oneliner.t: Democratic former two-term North Carolina governor (2017–2025) and four-term attorney general (2001–2017) from Nash County, who won the March 3, 2026 primary with 92% and faces Republican Michael Whatley for the open seat of retiring Sen. Thom Tillis.

born.t: June 13, 1957, Nashville, North Carolina (age 68 in March 2026 per AP, consistent)

profile.residence: Nashville, NC (hometown as listed by Fox News; current residence not documented)

upbringing.t: Cooper grew up in Nash County in eastern North Carolina, attended public schools there and worked summers on his parents' tobacco farm. His father, Roy Asberry Cooper II, was a lawyer and Democratic operative who co-chaired Gov. Jim Hunt's 1976 campaign; his mother, Beverly, was a teacher. He graduated from Northern Nash High School in 1975, then went to UNC-Chapel Hill as a Morehead Scholar (B.A. political science, 1979) and UNC law school (J.D., 1982). He joined his father's law firm in 1982 and won a state House seat in 1986. He married Kristin Bernhardt in 1992; they have three daughters, and he is an elder at White Memorial Presbyterian Church.

education.school: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

career.org: Fields, Cooper & Henderson (Nashville, NC; co-founded by his father)

career.role: State Representative; House Judiciary chair from 1989
State Senator (appointed to a vacancy, then elected); Majority Leader 1997–2001

platform.t: Campaign centerpiece is a 'Make Stuff Cost Less' plan: ban grocery stores from using algorithms to charge some customers more, stronger antitrust rules, and separate plans on child care, housing and energy costs.
Says trade authority belongs to Congress and has pledged to vote to roll back Trump's tariffs.

Would restore the enhanced ACA tax credits, reverse the 2025 Medicaid cuts, cap drug costs, and bar insurers from denying coverage a doctor says is needed; points to the 2023 Medicaid expansion he signed.
Wants to 'recreate FEMA' and says western North Carolina has received only a fraction of the Helene recovery money it needs.
Opposes the Iran war as waged, questions the exit strategy and says Congress should take back its constitutional war-declaring authority.

Acknowledges the southern border has been tightened, supports deporting violent criminals, and called for 'immediate reforms' to ICE operations before more funding; as governor vetoed sheriff-ICE cooperation bills in 2019, 2022 and 2024.
Supports background checks and red-flag laws and has said Congress should ban assault weapons.
Vetoed North Carolina's 12-week abortion ban in 2023 (overridden).
Said in December 2025 he would support banning stock trades by top federal officials.
Says he would work with Trump when he can and oppose him when needed, and frames the race partly as Congress acting as a check.
Opposes sending public money to private schools without accountability; vetoed a voucher expansion as governor.
Opposes new voting barriers; vetoed a 2018 voter ID bill and 2023 absentee-voting restrictions.

promises.t: Vote to roll back the tariffs.
Restore the enhanced ACA premium tax credits and reverse the 2025 Medicaid cuts.
Ban grocery stores from using algorithms to charge some customers more.
Bar insurers from denying coverage a doctor says is needed.
Recreate FEMA and secure more Helene recovery money for western North Carolina.
Support a ban on stock trading by top federal officials.
Push to end the Iran war and reassert Congress's war powers.

claims.claim: Born and raised in Nash County, attended public schools and worked summers on the family farm.

record.t: Born in Nashville, Nash County; Nash County public schools; summers on his parents' tobacco farm.

claims.claim: Earned undergraduate and law degrees from UNC-Chapel Hill.
Practiced law in Rocky Mount, representing everyday people and small businesses.

record.t: He practiced at his father's firm, Fields, Cooper & Henderson, from 1982. Wikipedia places the firm in Nashville, NC. The Rocky Mount location and client mix were not independently confirmed.

claims.claim: He and his wife Kristin raised three daughters; his mother was a public-school teacher.

record.t: Married Kristin Bernhardt in 1992; three daughters. Mother Beverly Cooper was a teacher.

claims.claim: Taught Sunday School for years and tutored students in local public schools.

record.t: Wikipedia records that he has taught Sunday school as a deacon and elder at White Memorial Presbyterian. The tutoring part rests only on his own account.

claims.claim: Wrote North Carolina's first children's health insurance initiative as a legislator.
claims.short: Wrote first child health insurance law

record.t: NC General Assembly bill records were not retrieved, so authorship could not be checked.

claims.claim: Was elected Attorney General and served four consecutive terms.

record.t: Elected AG in 2000 and re-elected in 2004, 2008 and 2012; served Jan. 2001 to Jan. 2017, the longest AG tenure in state history.

claims.claim: As AG he oversaw a 'sharp decrease in crime' and recovered billions of dollars for North Carolinians.

record.t: SBI/FBI crime data and AG recovery totals were not retrieved. The record does document a 2010 audit he ordered that found SBI lab agents had withheld information in about 230 cases over two decades.

claims.claim: Elected governor in 2016 and re-elected in 2020, both years Donald Trump carried North Carolina.

record.t: Beat Gov. Pat McCrory 49.02%–48.80% in 2016 (10,227 votes) and Lt. Gov. Dan Forest 51.52%–47.01% in 2020. Trump's North Carolina wins in those years are certified results, but no separate source was opened for them.

claims.claim: Reached a bipartisan agreement to expand Medicaid.

record.t: On March 27, 2023 he signed a Medicaid expansion law passed by the Republican legislature. A federal judge had blocked his 2017 attempt to expand by executive action.

claims.claim: Medicaid expansion brought health care to more than 650,000 North Carolinians by early 2025.

record.t: Wikipedia cites a pre-launch estimate of more than 600,000 eligible. NC DHHS enrollment data was not retrieved.

claims.claim: Enacted a plan to incentivize hospitals to relieve more than $4 billion in medical debt for 2 million residents.

record.t: No state or independent source on the program's results was retrieved.

claims.claim: Has won every election he entered over nearly 40 years in public service.

said.where: campaign message as reported on primary night

record.t: AP: he has not lost a North Carolina election since first running for the state House in the mid-1980s. Wikipedia's election history (1986 House primary through the 2026 Senate primary) shows no losses.

claims.claim: Western North Carolina has still received only about 15% of the federal funding it needs for Helene recovery.

record.t: The 15% figure depends on a needs estimate (probably the state's damage assessment) that was not retrieved. WLOS did not check it.

claims.claim: Whatley lobbied for utilities including Duke Energy while electric bills rose.

record.t: Whatley was executive vice president of the Consumer Energy Alliance until 2019, and Spectrum reports Duke Energy was a CEA client during his tenure. Spectrum's review of 12 years of lobbying reports found $1.2M of $3.5M tied to energy clients. No filing showing Whatley personally registered to lobby for Duke was cited.

claims.claim: Michael Whatley spent his career lobbying for Big Oil and utility companies, profiting while North Carolinians paid more.

said.where: TV ad 'Guys Like Him' (campaign release 2026-09-30; spend not reported, the only Cooper ad release found)

record.t: He lobbied for oil and gas clients at HBW Resources and was EVP of the industry-funded Consumer Energy Alliance (2008–2019), more than a decade in all. But his career also includes a federal clerkship, Energy Department and Senate staff jobs and party chairmanships, so 'spent his career' overstates it. 'Profiting while North Carolinians paid more' is a characterization.

said.t: Called for taking federal funds to expand Medicaid (repeated 2019).

did.t: Signed the bipartisan Medicaid expansion law.

said.t: Called for repealing HB2 and, as AG, refused to defend it as unconstitutional.

did.t: Signed a deal that repealed HB2 but imposed a three-year ban on local nondiscrimination ordinances.

said.t: Said voter ID solves a problem that doesn't exist.
Said a bill requiring sheriffs to honor ICE detainers sought to use 'fear to divide North Carolina.'

did.t: Vetoed sheriff-ICE cooperation bills in 2019, 2022 and 2024. The requirement later became law as part of a voucher-expansion package.

complicating.t: The repeal came with a three-year moratorium on local nondiscrimination ordinances, part of a compromise with the Republican legislature.

promises_prev.promise: Expand Medicaid by accepting federal funds.

evidence.t: Signed the expansion law on March 27, 2023.

complicating.t: A federal judge blocked his January 2017 attempt to expand without the legislature. Expansion came six years later, through a law the Republican legislature passed.

entries.t: Rated B by NORML; supported decriminalizing medical marijuana.
Supported allowing concealed carry while keeping gun restrictions.
Called for an assault weapons ban.
Supported pausing Syrian refugee admissions for screening.
Calls for ICE reforms before more funding while backing deportation of violent criminals.

His campaign pointed to his record as governor: he signed anti-BDS legislation, wrote the IHRA definition of antisemitism into state law, and hosted the Executive Mansion's first Passover Seder and Menorah Lighting. It called Whatley's attacks on that record false.

legal.t: Republican AG opponent Dan Boyce, his father Gene Boyce and two relatives' law firm sued Cooper and his campaign committee for defamation over a 2000 TV ad saying Boyce's firm charged taxpayers $28,000 an hour in a class-action tax case. A trial court dismissed the case in 2001. The N.C. Court of Appeals reversed (153 N.C. App. 25), holding that the complaint adequately alleged defamation per se and actual malice. The case went to the Court of Appeals three times. On April 16, 2014, shortly before trial, Cooper settled: his side (with its insurers, per AP) paid $75,000 plus mediation fees, and he and aide Julia White signed an apology saying that if the ad implied anything improper, they were wrong.
legal.status: Settled April 16, 2014 ($75,000 plus mediation fees, with signed apology); no finding of liability
